To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“The International Council for the Expedition of the Sea (ICE), the Directorate General for Fish (DG FISH), the Norwegian Institute of marine research (IMR), the Swedish Agency for marine and water management (SwAM) changed their formal coordination structures into organizations with geographical focus on marine ecosystem.

“The International Council for the Examination of the Sea (ICMS), the Directorate General for Fisheries and Maritime Affairs of the European Commission (DG FISH), the Norwegian Institute of marine research (IMR) and the Swedish agency for Marine and Water management (SwAM) adapted their sectoral structures to the new Ecosystem Approach to management (EAM) and a changing institutional environment by changing their formal coordination structures into organizations with geographical focus on marine ecosystem.

the International Council for Exploration of the Sea, DG FISH, IMR, and SwAM have changed their formal coordination structures from sectorally to geographically oriented organizations in order to adapt to a changing institutional and political context.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of formal coordination structures in marine governance, and how these structures change over time.
the organizational adaptation to an emerging EAM in Europe.
the organizational adaptation of public organizations to a new policy regime, and the role of organizational isomorphism in the diffusion of EAM in marine governance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the organizational changes in ICES, DG FISH, IMR, and SwAM are driven by a complex interaction of institutional and environmental forces, which are difficult to isolate from each other.
the sectoral organizations are converging in the direction of a more integrated and holistic approach, and that this convergence is a consequence of the changing institutional environment.
the sectoral structures in fisheries and marine governance in Europe are converging towards a geographical focus on regional marine areas.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sectoral structures of fisheries and marine environmental authorities have been transformed into geographical structures in the context of a new marine policy paradigm.
the EAM has been a catalyst for the organizational change.

the changes in the formal coordination structures of the four case organizations reflect a process of organizational adaptation to a new institutional environment and a new approach to management of fisheries and marine environmental resources.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the formal sectoral boundaries in marine governance are increasingly being challenged by a growing number of organizations in the European Union and beyond.
the formal coordination structures of public organizations involved with fisheries and marine environmental governance have become more similar over time.
the EAM and the associated institutional changes in the European marine governance system have been a driving force in the development of new forms of public sector organization.
